stem: When counseling a pediatric transplant candidate's family about transplantation risks before listing, which outcome is explicitly included in standard risk teaching?

options.text: Death may occur while on the transplant waiting list
Waitlist mortality never occurs for pediatric candidates
Death risk is limited to the first 24 hours after implantation only
Listing eliminates all mortality risk before transplant surgery

explanation.rationale_correct: Transplant risk education includes death as a risk on the waiting list, during surgery, and following transplantation.

rationale_incorrect.B: Waitlist mortality is explicitly listed among transplantation risks.
rationale_incorrect.C: Death risk is not confined to the first day after implantation; waitlist and later periods are also discussed.
rationale_incorrect.D: Listing does not eliminate pretransplant mortality risk.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → §6. Risks associated with transplantation → a. Death → i.

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → §6. Risks associated with transplantation → a. Death (waitlist, surgery, post-transplant); PDF p. 98 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Third pediatric-tagged item; distinct 010100 angle from cctc-1006/1015; anchor verified on Cupples p. 98.

stem: During living donor education, a potential donor expresses concern about emotional effects after donation. Which psychosocial risk should the coordinator include in teaching?

options.text: Guaranteed permanent elimination of all future stress
Mandatory loss of employment after every donation
Absence of any psychosocial risks because donors are prescreened

explanation.rationale_correct: Living donor psychosocial education includes risks such as postdonation depression or anxiety, body image concerns, and distress if the recipient has complications.

rationale_incorrect.B: Donor education discusses psychosocial risks rather than guaranteeing permanent stress elimination.
rationale_incorrect.C: Employment loss is not a universal mandatory outcome of donation.
rationale_incorrect.D: Psychosocial risks remain part of donor education despite medical prescreening.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 7, Living Donation → donor education → item 11 (psychosocial risks) → b.

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 7 → living donor education → item 11 (psychosocial risks including depression/anxiety); PDF p. 341 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Distinct 010300 angle from cctc-1007/1016; anchor verified on Cupples p. 341.

stem: A coordinator is updating post-transplant infection-prevention teaching materials. Evaluate the following statements:

elements.text: Recipients should avoid individuals with known infection when possible.
Recipients should avoid crowded areas when community influenza rates are high.
Consuming raw or undercooked eggs is recommended for immunosuppressed recipients.
Frequent hand-washing is a best practice to prevent infection.

explanation.rationale_correct: Infection-prevention teaching includes avoiding known infection contacts, crowded areas during high influenza activity, and frequent hand hygiene. Raw or undercooked eggs are not recommended.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement IV is also true—hand-washing is emphasized as a best practice.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statement III is false; dietary teaching advises against raw or undercooked eggs.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement III is false; not all four statements are correct.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → e. Infection prevention → ii. Airborne infections and iii. Dietary precautions
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Avoid individuals with known infection … Avoid crowded areas … Do not consume raw eggs

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → e. Infection prevention → ii. Airborne infections and iii. Dietary precautions (statements I–III); PDF p. 116 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → e. Infection prevention → i. Hand hygiene (statement IV); PDF p. 115 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Synthesized item. Statements I–II and IV from Cupples pp. 115–116; fifth complex_combo in bank.

stem: A lung recipient planning extensive travel two weeks after discharge asks whether this is advisable. What teaching aligns with standard early post-discharge guidance?

options.text: Extensive travel should be avoided immediately after discharge because close monitoring and unplanned visits may be needed
Long-distance travel is encouraged before the first clinic follow-up
Travel restrictions apply only to international flights longer than 12 hours
Recipients may discontinue immunosuppression during travel to reduce infection risk

explanation.rationale_correct: Early discharge education advises against extensive travel immediately after discharge due to the need for close monitoring, potential unplanned tests or clinic visits, and possible readmission.

rationale_incorrect.B: Early post-discharge guidance discourages extensive travel before stable follow-up.
rationale_incorrect.C: Travel guidance is not limited to a specific flight duration threshold.
rationale_incorrect.D: Immunosuppression must continue as prescribed; travel does not justify stopping therapy.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → §h. Communication → iv. Travel
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Patients should not travel extensively immediately after discharge

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → §h. Communication with the transplant team → iv. Travel; PDF p. 111 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Third lung organ tag; anchor verified on Cupples p. 111.
